items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: In fact the last concert we just did two months ago, Med Flory, things just happen in my band that start off something with an audience rapport, they happen immediately.

ctx.x: And colleges are buying them left and right. I was just doing a clinic and a few of the college people said, “Are you kidding, we ordered fourteen.” Because they don’t write arrangements like that anymore. They’re just straight ahead swing music. And especially if you want to show the band off, if you play the arrangements like it’s really written, because I actually patterned the band after the Benny Goodman band because Benny played in and out. Because it didn’t blend with the section. It did, but it would…

better, he still forgot to turn the page over, so he came in again, and I have to play after that, the vibes play. Then comes the clarinet. So he’s picking up the clarinet and he’s playing all alone while I’m playing my solo. Then he realizes what he’s doing. Once again the audience fell out, and you know what? That was the standard thing through the whole hour and a half we do. I’d asked Med, “Med, you want to sing?” “Anything you want, Terry.” And Med’s very funny. All the guys. You know I play straight man for…

items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And it’s sort of like my band is always partying anyhow. When we get together it’s a party. Because I like to laugh and like I said, I’ll play straight for Jack Sheldon, Frank Rossolino, Conte Candoli, Med Flory, these are funny minds.

ctx.x: Well I’ve really enjoyed this and I want to close with the last thing you wrote in your book, and it said, “Even though we know that into each life a little rain must fall, all in all I’ve been very fortunate for I’ve been able to laugh all the way to the bandstand.”

Yeah well it’s true. It really is true, Monk. I’ve been fortunate. ‘Cause I looked forward to getting on stage. I’m at my most comfortable when I’m on stage. Because I don’t work, I have fun. I mean I include my audience, that’s why I don’t like playing big concerts. If I play for people playing in a ballroom at least the audience is close, they’re about two feet away from me so I can tell the guy to get a toupee or whatever, I’m going to tell the guy. Lady get your nose fixed, or whatever it is. I become Don…
Well you figured out how to make it all work and I really admire it. And you’ve made some wonderful —
